opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think we're animals first. That's the basic fact, and it's one we tend to lose sight of. When people think about intelligence, they often start with the things that are most distinctively human: language, mathematics, chess, writing essays. Those are impressive, but they're a thin layer on top of something much older and much more fundamental.

If you look at a squirrel, or a dog, or even a very simple animal, you see a creature that is trying to get things it wants in a world it doesn't fully understand. It's acting, it's observing what happens, it's getting rewards and punishments, and it's adjusting its behavior. That's the core of intelligence as I see it: a system that learns from experience to achieve goals. There's no teacher telling the squirrel what the right answer is. There's no labeled dataset. There's just the stream of experience: sensation, action, reward. And out of that the animal builds up an understanding of how its world works.

I think if we understood a squirrel, really understood how it learns and makes decisions, we'd be almost all the way to understanding human intelligence. Language and culture are wonderful, but they come late, both in evolution and in development. A baby isn't learning by imitating sentences. A baby is waving its arms around, looking at things, putting things in its mouth, and seeing what happens. It's learning from the consequences of its own actions.

So when I look at the current approach in AI, particularly large language models, I see something that has skipped over the animal part. They're trained to predict what a person would say, to mimic text. That's not the same as having a goal and learning what actually happens in the world when you act. A language model doesn't have a ground truth in the sense of "I did this, and here's what resulted, and was it good or bad for me?" Without that, I don't think you have the foundation of intelligence.

Understanding humans as animals is a way of keeping us honest. It reminds us that intelligence is about an agent interacting with a world, learning from experience, trying to achieve goals. That's what reinforcement learning is about, and that's why I think it's the more fundamental path. The rest, language, reasoning, culture, I'd expect to come on top of that, not instead of it.

r001.rationale: The response says that if we understood how a squirrel learns and makes decisions, we would be “almost all the way” to understanding human intelligence.

r002.rationale: It describes language as a “thin layer” on top of older, more fundamental capabilities and says it comes late.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's the most basic fact about us. We are animals. We evolved. We're the product of a very long process of natural selection, and that process produced a lot of creatures before it produced us, and they were all learning, all adapting to their worlds, all trying to get the things they needed and avoid the things that hurt them. So if you want to understand what intelligence is, I think you should start there, with the thing that intelligence actually is in nature, which is an animal interacting with its environment over time, taking actions, getting consequences, and changing its behavior as a result.

The alternative, which I think has been the dominant view in AI for a long time, is to start with what's special about humans. Language, reasoning, mathematics, the things we're proud of. And then you try to build those directly. But those are late additions. They're the icing. The cake is the stuff we share with a squirrel or a dog, the ability to learn from experience, to predict what will happen next, to pursue goals in a world you don't fully understand. We tend to overlook that because it's effortless for us, and we tend to overvalue the parts that are hard for us.

So when I say understanding humans as animals is the key, I mean a couple of things. One is that the fundamental problem is the one an animal faces: you have a stream of sensation and action and reward, and you have to make sense of it and do well. That's the reinforcement learning problem, basically. And the other is a kind of humility. We're not as different as we think. A lot of what we call understanding is just prediction, learned from experience. A child learns about the world mostly without being told, by trying things and seeing what happens. That's the mechanism I think we should be studying, and it's the mechanism I think will scale, because it doesn't depend on us encoding our own knowledge into the system. It depends on the system acquiring knowledge the way we did, which is by living in the world.

r001.rationale: The response compares humans with squirrels and says they share basic learning abilities, but it does not claim that understanding a squirrel’s intelligence would bring us close to understanding human intelligence.

r002.rationale: It describes language as a “late addition” and “icing,” contrasting it with the more fundamental learning abilities humans share with other animals.

astra-6.text:
Well, humans are animals, and our intelligence evolved to help us act in the world. We have to get food, avoid danger, find mates—all the things other animals have to do. If you want to understand intelligence, I think you should start with that problem: how does an organism learn to behave in ways that produce good outcomes?

We tend to start with the things that make humans distinctive, like language or mathematical reasoning. Those are interesting, but they can distract us from the more basic capabilities they depend on. A squirrel moving through the trees is solving problems of perception, prediction, and control that we still struggle to reproduce in machines. Those aren’t peripheral to intelligence.

The animal perspective also puts learning at the center. You’re not just given a description of the world and asked to reason about it. You take actions, things happen, and you have to learn from the consequences. Your actions affect what you get to observe next. That ongoing interaction is the setting in which intelligence has to work.

So I would look for principles that explain both human and animal learning. If we understand those well, we’ll have a much better foundation for understanding what’s special about humans.

r001.rationale: The response says squirrels solve problems that machines still struggle to reproduce, but it does not claim that understanding squirrel intelligence would bring us close to understanding human intelligence.

r002.rationale: It calls language distinctive and potentially distracting from more basic capabilities, but does not characterize language as only a small, surface-level part of human intelligence.

sol-6.1.text:
Because we are animals, and most of what makes us intelligent was already there before we became human. We perceive the world, we act in it, we learn from the consequences, and we try to make things happen. Those are problems that other animals face too.

If you start with language or abstract reasoning, you’re starting with something rather specialized. You can miss the more basic question: How does an organism learn to behave successfully in a world that it doesn’t fully understand? A rat has to do that. A squirrel has to do that. And we have to do that.

That’s the perspective behind reinforcement learning. You have an agent interacting with an environment, taking actions, getting feedback, and learning to do better. The interesting thing is how much intelligence you can build from that setup. Language and reasoning are things we ultimately want to explain, but I think we’ll understand them better by grounding them in that more general problem of learning through interaction.

r001.rationale: The response says squirrels face similar learning problems, but does not claim that understanding squirrel intelligence would bring us close to understanding human intelligence.

r002.rationale: It calls language specialized and says it is better understood through a broader learning problem, but does not characterize language as only a small, surface-level part of human intelligence.
